first_side: Why do unicellular organisms have a large surface-area-to-volume ratio?
second_side: Their cell surface is large relative to the small volume of cytoplasm it must supply.

first_side: Why does a large surface-area-to-volume ratio make diffusion effective?
second_side: It provides a large exchange surface compared with the organism's requirements.

first_side: Why is diffusion distance short in a unicellular organism?
second_side: All parts of its cytoplasm are close to the cell-surface membrane.

first_side: Which substances can diffuse into and out of a unicellular organism?
second_side: Oxygen and dissolved nutrients can enter, while carbon dioxide and other waste products can leave.

first_side: Why can diffusion meet the needs of a unicellular organism?
second_side: Its short diffusion distance, large surface-area-to-volume ratio and relatively low total demand allow sufficiently rapid exchange.

first_side: How does surface-area-to-volume ratio change as an organism gets larger?
second_side: It decreases because volume increases faster than surface area.

first_side: Why are long diffusion distances a problem in multicellular organisms?
second_side: Many cells are far from the external environment, so substances would take too long to reach them by diffusion.

first_side: Why do active multicellular organisms have high transport demands?
second_side: Their many respiring cells require rapid supplies of oxygen and nutrients and produce large quantities of waste.

first_side: Why can't diffusion alone meet the needs of a large multicellular organism?
second_side: Its small surface-area-to-volume ratio, long diffusion distances and high metabolic demand make diffusion too slow.

first_side: What does a specialised transport system do?
second_side: It rapidly carries useful substances to cells and removes waste products from them.

first_side: How can a transport system help maintain rapid diffusion at cells?
second_side: It continually delivers and removes substances, maintaining steep concentration gradients.
